title: Enhancing lighting design through the investigation of illuminance and correlated color Temperature's effects on brain activity: An EEG-VR approach
research_question: Will brain activity features (i.e., EEG data) be modulated in a predictable fashion during the first seconds of exposure to varied illuminance levels (RQ1a) and CCT (RQ1b)? Will it be possible to associate specific EEG patterns with specific lighting conditions, in terms of illumination and CCT (RQ2)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' subjective mood responses (RQ3a: pleasure, RQ3b: arousal)? Will EEG measurements during the first few seconds of observing an indoor environment with different illumination and CCT conditions predict participants' behavioral choices of desired vs. non-desired lighting (RQ4)?

participants.description: 25 healthy adult participants (out of 33 recruited, 8 excluded due to technical problems) associated with Cornell University. 21 undergraduate students, 4 graduate students/faculty. 15 female, 10 male. Age range 18-64 years (mean 24.4, SD 8.3). All affirmed no medical eye problems, no difficulty distinguishing colors. 64% used eyeglasses/contact lenses. All reported 7-9h sleep prior to experiment.
participants.recruitment: convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and announcements on departmental e-mail lists)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A modern interior office room (4.0 m × 7.4 m x 3.0 m) designed in Autodesk 3ds Max and Unreal Engine 4.26. Participants experienced the virtual environment from a seated position at a desk using a Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display (1832 × 1920 pixels per eye, max brightness 100 nits). 17 different artificial lighting conditions were tested, selected from a matrix of 7 illumination levels (300lm to 4500lm) and 7 CCT levels (1500 K to 7500 K). Conditions included neutral illumination (2400lm) across all CCTs, neutral CCT (4500K) across all illuminations, and four quadrant conditions (low/high illumination with low/high CCT).

mechanisms: Mental effects of light through non-image-forming pathways
Stimulation of brain areas involved in emotional processing (medial amygdala, lateral habenula)
Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin as primary drivers for non-image-forming effects of light
Frontal brain regions involved in higher-order cognitive processing (working memory, executive action, decision-making)
Parietal brain regions associated with spatial perception and environmental information processing
implementation_implications: Assist architects and engineers in developing lighting plans optimized according to occupants' subjective states (brain activity, lighting adjustment behavior, mood).
Leverage VR simulations in AEC sector to assess lighting design choices, potentially eliminating need for expensive physical mock-ups.
Potential development of brain-computer interfaces (BCI) for automatic lighting adjustment based on user's brain responses.
Tailoring lighting settings in interior spaces using brain responses for optimizing occupant productivity and wellbeing.
Applications in treatments like direct light therapy for mood disorders.
Empowering disabled individuals to control lighting through BCIs for easier environmental interaction.
Combining BCI with VR for fluid interaction with virtual environments and testing interaction systems for real-world spaces.
Evidence-based design approaches using VR for lighting evaluation can be more inexpensive and accessible, leading to larger comparative datasets.

limitations: Limited luminance range of VR HMDs compared to real-world light sources, diminishing usefulness at very high and very low illuminance extremes.
VR experience does not accurately reflect blinding effects or glare of real-world lighting.
VR HMDs' minimum displayable intensities are too high to reliably study scotopic vision range, color shifts, and diminished visual acuity in very low-light environments.
Infeasibility of studying simulated natural light using current VR technology.
Illumination measures (lumens) not validated against standard real-world procedures (lux) and not directly transferable to real-world settings.
Participant reactions in VR environments may not precisely reflect real-world contexts.
High attrition rate due to loss of data from multiple participants (corrupted/unusable EEG data, unprinted timestamps, HMD/EEG battery crashes).
Human error on the part of the researchers during the experiment.
Convenience sample composed mostly of undergraduate students at Cornell University.
Did not evaluate demographic variables (e.g., age, gender) or other factors (e.g., participant sleep schedules, time of day) that may impact results.
Number of electrodes used and EEG device may affect quality of brain activity measurements and conclusions.
